_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla, typed out on the slip. Each lesson has two: "start" comes on as the lesson opens, and "check" is a short quiz once the lesson's check is done. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies" (none means a plain "Roger. Over."). A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. Autumn, and the Pacific is lining up storms like boxcars on a siding. This week you put it all together and follow one storm from start to finish: barometer, wind, and every cloud from the first cirrus to the last shower.

replies.say: The workbook has a chapter on radar.
replies.back: Some fellow’s notion for the future, I expect. Read it anyway.

turns.them: By the end you should read a storm two days off. Questions at the end.
Harrow, Walla Walla. Questions. A storm goes by. When does the barometer stop falling and start to climb?

replies.back: The squall goes through, the wind swings northwest, and up she goes.
No, it’s still falling then. It bottoms out at the cold front and climbs behind it.
It steadies there, but it doesn’t climb until the cold front has gone by.

turns.them: Stand with your back to the wind. Where is the low?

replies.back: Right. Buys Ballot’s rule, from the Dutchman who wrote it down in 1857.
Other side. With your back to the wind, low pressure is on your left.
The wind circles a low rather than blowing into it. Back to the wind, the low is on your left.

turns.them: Which hour is the worst to be flying through?

replies.say: Under the cold front’s squall line.
replies.back: Gusts, towers, maybe hail. Sit that hour out in the hangar.

replies.say: In the warm front’s steady rain.
replies.back: Low and wet, but smooth. It’s the cold front’s line of towers that bites.
Mild and muggy there. It’s the cold front’s line of towers that bites.

turns.them: That’s a whole storm read. One more lesson, for the winter.
